claim: Layer 2 of the rat dorsal presubiculum is composed of two principal cell populations: calbindin-positive and calbindin-negative neurons.
source: In L2, calbindin immunoreactivity (Fujise et al., 1995) revealed two distinct principal cell populations - calbindin-positive and calbindin-negative neurons - which represented ~33% and 67% of the total neurons within this layer, respectively (n = 916 calbindin-positive out of 2793 NeuN-positive neurons; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data showing calbindin and NeuN staining, with quantitative cell counts provided (916 calbindin-positive out of 2793 NeuN-positive neurons), and referenced to Figure 1B.

claim: Calbindin-positive PreS layer 2 neurons are arranged in clusters.
source: Similarly to the organization of MEC (Varga et al., 2010; Kitamura et al., 2014; Ray et al., 2014; Fuchs et al., 2016), calbindin-positive PreS L2 neurons were also arranged in clusters, and their dendrites bundled together and formed tent-like structures in layer 1 (L1; Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical observations shown in Figure 1B and comparison to similar organization in MEC from cited studies.

claim: The PreS projection to MEC is layer-specific, with the large majority of retrogradely-labelled neurons found in ipsilateral PreS layer 3.
source: In line with previous work (Caballero‐Bleda and Witter, 1993; Honda and Ishizuka, 2004), we found that the PreS projection to MEC is layer-specific, since the large majority of retrogradely-labelled neurons was found in ipsilateral (and contralateral; not shown) PreS L3 (Figure 1C,D; 4497 total counted neurons, n = 4 brains).
evidence: The claim is supported by retrograde tracing data with quantitative cell counts (4497 total counted neurons, n = 4 brains) shown in Figure 1C,D, and is consistent with previous cited studies.

claim: Labeling in PreS layer 2 following MEC tracer injection was sparse, with very few neurons contributing to this pathway.
source: On the other hand, labeling in L2 was sparse, with very few neurons contributing to this pathway (Figure 1D), all of which were calbindin-negative (not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1D and additional observation about calbindin expression.

claim: The majority of retrogradely-labelled neurons in contralateral PreS layer 2 following PreS tracer injection was calbindin-positive (~76%).
source: CTB injections in PreS resulted in dense cellular labeling in contralateral PreS L2 (Figure 1E; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–D; van Groen and Wyss, 1990a; Honda et al., 2008), where the majority of retrogradely-labelled neurons was calbindin-positive (~76%, Figure 1F; 159 total counted L2 neurons, n = 3 brains) and arranged in clusters (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by retrograde tracing data with quantitative analysis (159 total counted L2 neurons, n = 3 brains) shown in Figure 1E,F, and is consistent with previous cited studies.

claim: Following tracer injections in retrosplenial cortex area 29, the majority of retrogradelly-labelled neurons in PreS layer 2 were calbindin-negative (~86%).
source: CTB injections centered on this area resulted in intense cellular labeling in the contralateral homotypical area (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3E–H). Within PreS, most retrogradelly-labelled neurons were found within L2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E–H), the majority of which were calbindin-negative (~86%, Figure 1G; 896 total counted L2 neurons, n = 4 brains).
evidence: The claim is supported by retrograde tracing data with quantitative analysis (896 total counted L2 neurons, n = 4 brains) shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3E–H.

claim: Calbindin-positive PreS layer 2 neurons project to the contralateral PreS.
source: CTB injections in PreS resulted in dense cellular labeling in contralateral PreS L2 (Figure 1E; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–D; van Groen and Wyss, 1990a; Honda et al., 2008), where the majority of retrogradely-labelled neurons was calbindin-positive (~76%, Figure 1F; 159 total counted L2 neurons, n = 3 brains) and arranged in clusters (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from retrograde tracing data showing that 76% of retrogradely-labeled neurons in contralateral PreS L2 are calbindin-positive, indicating these neurons project to contralateral PreS.

claim: Calbindin-negative PreS layer 2 neurons project to the contralateral retrosplenial cortex area 29.
source: CTB injections centered on this area resulted in intense cellular labeling in the contralateral homotypical area (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3E–H). Within PreS, most retrogradelly-labelled neurons were found within L2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E–H), the majority of which were calbindin-negative (~86%, Figure 1G; 896 total counted L2 neurons, n = 4 brains).
evidence: The claim is inferred from retrograde tracing data showing that 86% of retrogradely-labeled neurons in PreS L2 following RS29 injection are calbindin-negative, indicating these neurons project to contralateral RS29.

claim: A large proportion of PreS neurons (~60%) met the criteria for head-direction cells during passive rotation.
source: A large proportion of PreS neurons met these criteria (186 out of 310; ~60%; see also Boccara et al., 2010; Tukker et al., 2015; Figure 2A,B), with the fraction 'strong' HD cells (HD index >0.8 and p<0.01; 121/310, ~39%) being within the range of previous studies from freely-behaving rodents (Taube et al., 1990a; 1990b; Boccara et al., 2010; Tukker et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of 310 recorded neurons during passive rotation, with 186 meeting HD criteria, shown in Figure 2A,B, and compared to previous cited studies.

claim: Preferred firing directions of PreS HD cells were homogeneously distributed over a 360 degrees angle.
source: Firing in HD cells was stable over time, as assessed by Pearson's correlation coefficient of HD tuning curves computed for the two halves of each recording session (mean correlation coefficient, 0.79 ± 0.21; n = 181 HD cells) and preferred firing directions were homogeneously distributed over a 360 degrees angle (Figure 2C; Taube et al., 1990a; Taube, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of 181 HD cells shown in Figure 2C and is consistent with previous cited studies.

claim: Average firing rates of PreS HD cells during passive rotation were 3.4 ± 4.2 Hz.
source: During passive rotation, average and peak firing rates of HD cells (3.4 ± 4.2 Hz and 15.4 ± 12.6 Hz, respectively; n = 186) were also within the range reported during free behavior (Taube et al., 1990a; 1990b; Blair and Sharp, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from 186 HD cells during passive rotation and compared to previous cited studies.

claim: Peak firing rates of PreS HD cells during passive rotation were 15.4 ± 12.6 Hz.
source: During passive rotation, average and peak firing rates of HD cells (3.4 ± 4.2 Hz and 15.4 ± 12.6 Hz, respectively; n = 186) were also within the range reported during free behavior (Taube et al., 1990a; 1990b; Blair and Sharp, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from 186 HD cells during passive rotation and compared to previous cited studies.

claim: The general tuning properties of HD cells were very similar between passive-rotation and free behavior.
source: As shown in the representative recording in Figure 2D, the general tuning properties of the HD cells were very similar between passive-rotation and free behavior (Figure 2E; mean correlation coefficient of the HD tuning curves, 0.68 ± 0.20, p<0.05; n = 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequential recordings of the same HD cells (n=4) during both conditions, with quantitative correlation analysis shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: The majority of identified HD cells were located in layer 3 (n = 18).
source: The majority of identified HD cells were located in L3 (n = 18), the rest in deep layers (L4–6; n = 9). No HD cell was recovered in L2.
evidence: The claim is supported by juxtacellular labeling and recovery of 27 HD cells, with their laminar distribution quantified.

claim: No HD cell was recovered in layer 2 of the PreS.
source: The majority of identified HD cells were located in L3 (n = 18), the rest in deep layers (L4–6; n = 9). No HD cell was recovered in L2.
evidence: The claim is supported by juxtacellular labeling and recovery of 27 HD cells, with their laminar distribution quantified.

claim: All identified layer 3 principal neurons whose morphology could be assessed were classified as pyramidal (21 out of 21).
source: All principal neurons whose morphology could be assessed (see Materials and methods) were classified as pyramidal (21 out of 21 in L3; 4 out of 8 in deep layers) or multipolar neurons (4 out of 8 in deep layers).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis of 21 layer 3 principal neurons following juxtacellular labeling.

claim: Within the superficial PreS layer, HD responses are preferentially contributed by layer 3 pyramidal neurons.
source: These data thus indicate that, within the superficial PreS layer, HD responses are preferentially contributed by L3 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data showing that identified HD cells were predominantly found in L3 (18/25), none in L2, and all L3 principal neurons were pyramidal.

claim: A minority of fast-spiking interneurons (3 out of 20) contributed weak HD responses.
source: In line with previous work from freely-moving rats (Tukker et al., 2015) we found that a minority of FS interneurons (3 out of 20) contributed weak HD responses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), which were stable between the two halves of the recording sessions (mean correlation coefficient, 0.73 ± 0.30, p<0.05; n = 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of 20 FS interneurons, with 3 showing weak HD responses, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, and is consistent with previous cited work.

claim: The majority of fast-spiking interneurons (13 out of 20) were significantly modulated by angular velocity.
source: The majority of FS interneurons (13 out of 20) were significantly modulated by angular velocity (see Materials and methods) and fired at higher rates during rotation compared to resting periods (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of 20 FS interneurons showing angular velocity modulation, with data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Theta rhythmicity was very sparse among fast-spiking interneurons.
source: Theta rhythmicity was very sparse among FS interneurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E); yet classical 'theta-cells' were observed within the PreS (as in Taube et al., 1990a; Blair and Sharp, 1996), and one of them was identified as a paravalbumin-positive interneuron (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of theta rhythmicity in FS interneurons shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E, with comparison to previous cited studies.

claim: One identified theta-cell was a paravalbumin-positive interneuron.
source: Theta rhythmicity was very sparse among FS interneurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E); yet classical 'theta-cells' were observed within the PreS (as in Taube et al., 1990a; Blair and Sharp, 1996), and one of them was identified as a paravalbumin-positive interneuron (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by juxtacellular labeling and immunohistochemical identification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Eight long-range axonal projections from identified HD cells reached the ipsilateral MEC.
source: In total, 8 long-range axonal projections from identified HD cells could be recovered (median HD index, 0.9; range 0.64–0.96, n = 8; Figure 4D). All of them reached the ipsilateral MEC where they generally showed a layer-specific distribution: compared to L2/1 and deep layers, most axonal length was observed within MEC L3 (total axonal length, 2.19 ± 3.38 mm in L3 versus 0.44 ± 0.57 mm in L1, L2 and deep layers; n = 8, p=0.025; Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological reconstruction of 8 long-range axonal projections from identified HD cells, with quantitative measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Most axonal length from PreS HD cells in MEC was observed within MEC layer 3 (2.19 ± 3.38 mm in L3 versus 0.44 ± 0.57 mm in L1, L2 and deep layers; n = 8, p=0.025).
source: All of them reached the ipsilateral MEC where they generally showed a layer-specific distribution: compared to L2/1 and deep layers, most axonal length was observed within MEC L3 (total axonal length, 2.19 ± 3.38 mm in L3 versus 0.44 ± 0.57 mm in L1, L2 and deep layers; n = 8, p=0.025; Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of axonal length in different MEC layers from 8 reconstructed axons, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: HD inputs from PreS to MEC are arranged according to layer-specific gradients within the MEC.
source: Altogether, our data provide an anatomical demonstration that the MEC receives HD inputs from upstream PreS L3 neurons, and that HD inputs are arranged according to layer-specific gradients within the MEC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the quantitative analysis showing preferential axonal branching in MEC L3 from identified PreS HD cells.

claim: Both the strength of HD modulation and the proportion of HD cells were significantly lower in layer 2 compared to layer 3 (0/11 in L2 versus 18/25 in L3, p<0.001).
source: Both the strength of HD modulation (Figure 6C) and the proportion of HD cells were significantly lower in L2 compared to L3 (0/11 in L2 versus 18/25 in L3, p<0.001, Fisher's Exact Test).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison of identified neurons in L2 (n=11) and L3 (n=25), with statistical analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Average firing rates did not differ between layer 2 and layer 3 neurons (L2, 2.5 ± 2.5 Hz; L3, 2.4 ± 2.6 Hz; p=0.245).
source: Notably, while average firing rates did not differ (L2, 2.5 ± 2.5 Hz; L3, 2.4 ± 2.6 Hz; p=0.245), spiking rhythmicity in the theta-frequency range (4–12 Hz) as assessed by a standard 'theta index' (Yartsev et al., 2011) was more prominent among L2 than L3 neurons (Figure 6D,E; we note that in our head-fixed preparation, theta activity presumably reflects immobility-related type-II theta [Shin, 2010, Tai et al., 2012] since animals were not actively moving during passive rotation).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison of firing rates between L2 and L3 neurons with statistical analysis.

claim: Spiking rhythmicity in the theta-frequency range (4–12 Hz) was more prominent among layer 2 than layer 3 neurons.
source: Notably, while average firing rates did not differ (L2, 2.5 ± 2.5 Hz; L3, 2.4 ± 2.6 Hz; p=0.245), spiking rhythmicity in the theta-frequency range (4–12 Hz) as assessed by a standard 'theta index' (Yartsev et al., 2011) was more prominent among L2 than L3 neurons (Figure 6D,E; we note that in our head-fixed preparation, theta activity presumably reflects immobility-related type-II theta [Shin, 2010, Tai et al., 2012] since animals were not actively moving during passive rotation).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative theta index analysis shown in Figure 6D,E, with reference to the method from a cited study.

claim: The only statistically-significant theta-rhythmic discharges among principal neurons were selectively contributed by layer 2 cells (4 out of 4).
source: In line with previous work from freely-moving animals (Taube et al., 1990a; Boccara et al., 2010; Tukker et al., 2015), theta-rhythmicity was very sparse among principal neurons (Figure 6E), and the only statistically-significant theta-rhythmic discharges (as assessed by a shuffling procedure; see Materials and methods) were selectively contributed by L2 cells (4 out of 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of theta rhythmicity using a shuffling procedure, shown in Figure 6E, and is consistent with previous cited studies.

claim: Theta-rhythmic spiking patterns were contributed by both calbindin-positive and calbindin-negative layer 2 neurons.
source: Theta-rhythmic spiking patterns were contributed by both calbindin-positive and calbindin-negative neurons (Figure 6E), and average theta-indices did not differ significantly between the two cell classes (calbindin-positive, 2.3 ± 2.3, n = 3; calbindin-negative, 3.8 ± 2.5, n = 6; p=0.54; we note however that the small dataset of identified calbindin-positive neurons prevents rigorous assessment of structure-function relationships).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of theta indices in both calbindin-positive (n=3) and calbindin-negative (n=6) neurons, shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The spike waveforms of layer 2 neurons differed significantly from that of layer 3 cells, showing on average a significantly longer duration and more pronounced negativity.
source: Notably, the spike waveforms of L2 neurons differed significantly from that of L3 cells (Figure 6F), as they showed on average a significantly longer duration (as assessed by spike half-width) and more pronounced negativity (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of spike waveform features (half-width and negativity amplitude) shown in Figure 6F,G.

claim: PreS layer 2 and layer 3 neurons can be differentiated according to spike waveform features, HD modulation and temporal spiking properties within the theta-frequency range.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that PreS L2 and L3 neurons can be differentiated according to spike waveform features, HD modulation and temporal spiking properties within the theta-frequency range (see Figure 6 and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by multiple analyses shown in Figure 6, integrating spike waveform, HD modulation, and theta rhythmicity data.

claim: The PreS receives a major projection from dorsal thalamic nuclei.
source: The PreS receives a major projection from dorsal thalamic nuclei (Shipley and Sorensen, 1975; Thompson and Robertson, 1987; Shibata, 1993), contains the highest proportion of sharp HD cells among parahippocampal cortices (Boccara et al., 2010; Winter et al., 2015a) and contributes a major projection to the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) (Caballero‐Bleda and Witter, 1993; 1994; Honda and Ishizuka, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The PreS contains the highest proportion of sharp HD cells among parahippocampal cortices.
source: The PreS receives a major projection from dorsal thalamic nuclei (Shipley and Sorensen, 1975; Thompson and Robertson, 1987; Shibata, 1993), contains the highest proportion of sharp HD cells among parahippocampal cortices (Boccara et al., 2010; Winter et al., 2015a) and contributes a major projection to the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) (Caballero‐Bleda and Witter, 1993; 1994; Honda and Ishizuka, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous physiological studies.

claim: The PreS contributes a major projection to the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC).
source: The PreS receives a major projection from dorsal thalamic nuclei (Shipley and Sorensen, 1975; Thompson and Robertson, 1987; Shibata, 1993), contains the highest proportion of sharp HD cells among parahippocampal cortices (Boccara et al., 2010; Winter et al., 2015a) and contributes a major projection to the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) (Caballero‐Bleda and Witter, 1993; 1994; Honda and Ishizuka, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The PreS represents a major gateway of HD information into the entorhinal-hippocampal circuit.
source: Thus, the PreS represents a major gateway of HD information into the entorhinal-hippocampal circuit.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combination of PreS receiving thalamic HD inputs, containing high proportion of HD cells, and projecting to MEC, as described in the preceding sentences with citations.

claim: Grid cell firing was disrupted following inactivation of HD signals.
source: HD inputs to entorhinal grid cells could be 'un-masked' by removing excitatory feedback from the hippocampus (Bonnevie et al., 2013), and grid cell firing was disrupted following inactivation of HD signals (Winter et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: HD inputs to entorhinal grid cells could be 'un-masked' by removing excitatory feedback from the hippocampus.
source: HD inputs to entorhinal grid cells could be 'un-masked' by removing excitatory feedback from the hippocampus (Bonnevie et al., 2013), and grid cell firing was disrupted following inactivation of HD signals (Winter et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claim: Neurons coding for head-direction are crucial for spatial navigation.
source: Neurons coding for head-direction are crucial for spatial navigation.
evidence: The claim is a general statement based on established scientific knowledge about HD cells and their role in navigation.

claim: Layer 2 is composed of two principal cell populations (calbindin-positive and calbindin-negative neurons) which targeted the contralateral PreS and retrosplenial cortex, respectively.
source: We found that layer2 is composed of two principal cell populations (calbindin-positive and calbindin-negative neurons) which targeted the contralateral PreS and retrosplenial cortex, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by retrograde tracing experiments showing differential projection targets of calbindin-positive and calbindin-negative L2 neurons.

claim: Layer 3 pyramidal neurons projected to the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC).
source: Layer3 pyramidal neurons projected to the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC).
evidence: The claim is supported by retrograde tracing experiments showing that the majority of MEC-projecting neurons are in L3.

claim: Head-direction responses were preferentially contributed by layer 3 pyramidal cells.
source: By juxtacellularly recording PreS neurons in awake rats during passive-rotation, we found that head-direction responses were preferentially contributed by layer3 pyramidal cells, whose long-range axons branched within layer3 of the MEC.
evidence: The claim is supported by juxtacellular recordings and labeling showing that identified HD cells were predominantly L3 pyramidal neurons.

claim: Long-range axons of layer 3 pyramidal HD cells branched within layer 3 of the MEC.
source: By juxtacellularly recording PreS neurons in awake rats during passive-rotation, we found that head-direction responses were preferentially contributed by layer3 pyramidal cells, whose long-range axons branched within layer3 of the MEC.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological reconstruction of long-range axonal projections from identified L3 HD cells showing preferential branching in MEC L3.

claim: Layer 2 neurons displayed distinct spike-shapes compared to layer 3 neurons.
source: In contrast, layer2 neurons displayed distinct spike-shapes, were not modulated by head-direction but rhythmically-entrained by theta-oscillations.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of spike waveform features showing significant differences between L2 and L3 neurons.

claim: Layer 2 neurons were not modulated by head-direction.
source: In contrast, layer2 neurons displayed distinct spike-shapes, were not modulated by head-direction but rhythmically-entrained by theta-oscillations.
evidence: The claim is supported by juxtacellular recordings showing that 0/11 identified L2 neurons met HD criteria.

claim: Layer 2 neurons were rhythmically-entrained by theta-oscillations.
source: In contrast, layer2 neurons displayed distinct spike-shapes, were not modulated by head-direction but rhythmically-entrained by theta-oscillations.
evidence: The claim is supported by theta index analysis showing significantly higher theta rhythmicity in L2 compared to L3 neurons.

claim: Fast-spiking interneurons showed only weak directionality and theta-rhythmicity.
source: Fast-spiking interneurons showed only weak directionality and theta-rhythmicity, but were significantly modulated by angular velocity.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of 20 FS interneurons showing that only 3/20 showed weak HD responses and theta rhythmicity was sparse.

claim: Fast-spiking interneurons were significantly modulated by angular velocity.
source: Fast-spiking interneurons showed only weak directionality and theta-rhythmicity, but were significantly modulated by angular velocity.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis showing that 13/20 FS interneurons were significantly modulated by angular velocity.

claim: PreS neurons differentially contribute to head-direction coding.
source: Our data thus indicate that PreS neurons differentially contribute to head-direction coding, and point to a cell-type- and layer-specific routing of directional and non-directional information to downstream cortical targets.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement inferred from the combined data showing layer-specific differences in HD modulation.

claim: There is a cell-type- and layer-specific routing of directional and non-directional information to downstream cortical targets in the PreS.
source: Our data thus indicate that PreS neurons differentially contribute to head-direction coding, and point to a cell-type- and layer-specific routing of directional and non-directional information to downstream cortical targets.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined anatomical and physiological data showing that L3 HD cells project to MEC while L2 non-HD cells project to contralateral PreS and RS29.

claim: The cytoarchitectonic and functional architecture of PreS closely resembles that of the MEC.
source: These findings closely resemble the cytoarchitectonic and functional architecture of the MEC; specifically, also in MEC (i) calbindin-positive neurons are clustered and project (at least to some extent) to the contralateral homologue area (Varga et al., 2010; Fuchs et al., 2016), and (ii) L2 and L3 neurons differ in morphological, electrophysiological, functional properties and projection targets (Kitamura et al., 2014; Ray et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of the present findings with previous cited studies on MEC organization.

claim: In MEC, calbindin-positive neurons are clustered and project to the contralateral homologue area.
source: These findings closely resemble the cytoarchitectonic and functional architecture of the MEC; specifically, also in MEC (i) calbindin-positive neurons are clustered and project (at least to some extent) to the contralateral homologue area (Varga et al., 2010; Fuchs et al., 2016), and (ii) L2 and L3 neurons differ in morphological, electrophysiological, functional properties and projection targets (Kitamura et al., 2014; Ray et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on MEC organization.

claim: In MEC, layer 2 and layer 3 neurons differ in morphological, electrophysiological, functional properties and projection targets.
source: These findings closely resemble the cytoarchitectonic and functional architecture of the MEC; specifically, also in MEC (i) calbindin-positive neurons are clustered and project (at least to some extent) to the contralateral homologue area (Varga et al., 2010; Fuchs et al., 2016), and (ii) L2 and L3 neurons differ in morphological, electrophysiological, functional properties and projection targets (Kitamura et al., 2014; Ray et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on MEC organization.

claim: The common basic architecture of PreS and MEC circuits could point to similar mechanisms supporting the generation of spatial firing within these areas.
source: The common basic architecture of PreS and MEC circuits could point to similar mechanisms supporting the generation of spatial firing within these areas, as proposed by previous authors (Boccara et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the observed similarities between PreS and MEC organization, with reference to a previous proposal.

claim: The abundance and general properties of PreS HD neurons were very similar to the ones reported from freely-moving animals.
source: Our experiments confirmed earlier work which indicated that HD responses are largely preserved under these conditions (Zugaro et al., 2001; 2002; Shinder and Taube, 2011; 2014). Indeed, the abundance and general properties of PreS HD neurons were very similar to the ones reported from freely-moving animals, thus pointing to a largely intact HD system which is uncoupled from voluntary animal locomotion (see also Winter et al., 2015b).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of the present data with previous cited studies from freely-moving animals.

claim: The HD system is largely intact and uncoupled from voluntary animal locomotion during passive rotation.
source: Indeed, the abundance and general properties of PreS HD neurons were very similar to the ones reported from freely-moving animals, thus pointing to a largely intact HD system which is uncoupled from voluntary animal locomotion (see also Winter et al., 2015b).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similarity of HD properties between passive rotation and free behavior, with reference to a previous study.

claim: The lack of directionality in PreS layer 2 might be due to the lack of HD inputs from the dorsal thalamus.
source: We note that the lack of directionality in PreS L2 might be due to the lack of HD inputs from the dorsal thalamus, in line with tracing experiments indicating that thalamic inputs largely avoid PreS L2 (van Groen and Wyss, 1990b; 1995; Shibata, 1993).
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the observed lack of HD responses in L2 and previous cited tracing studies showing sparse thalamic inputs to L2.

claim: Thalamic inputs largely avoid PreS layer 2.
source: We note that the lack of directionality in PreS L2 might be due to the lack of HD inputs from the dorsal thalamus, in line with tracing experiments indicating that thalamic inputs largely avoid PreS L2 (van Groen and Wyss, 1990b; 1995; Shibata, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical tracing studies.

claim: Layer 2 neurons could contribute the spatial signals (grid and border cells) previously recorded in PreS.
source: An intriguing possibility is that L2 neurons could contribute the spatial signals which have been previously recorded among PreS units (i.e. grid and border cells; Boccara et al., 2010; Winter et al., 2015b).
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis based on the observation that L2 neurons are not HD cells, with reference to previous studies showing grid and border cells in PreS.

claim: Layer 2 could be the principal source of grid activity in PreS, as it is the case in MEC.
source: Based on the known correlation between spiking theta-rhythmicity and grid activity (Boccara et al., 2010; Brandon et al., 2011; Koenig et al., 2011) and the fact that under our recording configuration, theta-rhythmic responses were almost exclusively contributed by L2 PreS neurons (Figure 6D,E), we speculate that L2 could be the principal source of grid activity in PreS - as it is the case in MEC (Boccara et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is a speculative hypothesis based on the correlation between theta rhythmicity and grid activity from cited studies, and the observation that L2 neurons show theta rhythmicity.

claim: There is a known correlation between spiking theta-rhythmicity and grid activity.
source: Based on the known correlation between spiking theta-rhythmicity and grid activity (Boccara et al., 2010; Brandon et al., 2011; Koenig et al., 2011) and the fact that under our recording configuration, theta-rhythmic responses were almost exclusively contributed by L2 PreS neurons (Figure 6D,E), we speculate that L2 could be the principal source of grid activity in PreS - as it is the case in MEC (Boccara et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies showing correlation between theta rhythmicity and grid activity.

claim: The representation of HD appears to be much sparser in MEC layer 3 compared to its presynaptic input structure (PreS layer 3).
source: An intriguing observation is that the representation of HD appears to be much sparser in MEC L3 (Giocomo et al., 2014; Tang et al., 2015) compared to its presynaptic inputs structure (i.e. PreS L3), arguing against a simple feed-forward inheritance of HD coding.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the present findings with previous cited studies on HD representation in MEC L3.

claim: The sparse HD representation in MEC layer 3 argues against a simple feed-forward inheritance of HD coding.
source: An intriguing observation is that the representation of HD appears to be much sparser in MEC L3 (Giocomo et al., 2014; Tang et al., 2015) compared to its presynaptic inputs structure (i.e. PreS L3), arguing against a simple feed-forward inheritance of HD coding.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed difference in HD representation density between PreS L3 and MEC L3.

claim: The PreS might be critically involved in the stability of spatial representations.
source: Inactivation and lesion studies have indicated that the PreS might be critically involved in the stability of spatial representations (Taube et al., 1992; Goodridge and Taube, 1997; Calton et al., 2003; Taube, 2007) by binding visual landmark information to the HD representation (Vogt and Miller, 1983; McNaughton et al., 1991; Goodridge and Taube, 1995; Knierim et al., 1995; Taube, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous inactivation and lesion studies.

claim: The PreS binds visual landmark information to the HD representation.
source: Inactivation and lesion studies have indicated that the PreS might be critically involved in the stability of spatial representations (Taube et al., 1992; Goodridge and Taube, 1997; Calton et al., 2003; Taube, 2007) by binding visual landmark information to the HD representation (Vogt and Miller, 1983; McNaughton et al., 1991; Goodridge and Taube, 1995; Knierim et al., 1995; Taube, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on visual landmark processing in PreS.

claim: The connection from PreS layer 2 to RS cortex could point to layer 2 as the site where visual information is processed and integrated into the PreS HD map.
source: In this context, the connection from PreS L2 to RS cortex (Figure 1G) – an area known to receive strong direct inputs from primary visual cortex (Ding, 2013) – could point to L2 as the site where visual information is processed and integrated into the PreS HD map.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the anatomical connection between L2 and RS cortex, and the known visual inputs to RS cortex from a cited study.
